Dear Lofti,

Paul Vitanyi and others have developed the universal similarity based on
Kolmogorov complexity K. It has very general "optimality" properties
which justifies the label "universal". It has been applied to a wide
range of problems, from phylogenetic tree reconstruction, to similarity
of languages, and determining the composer of pieces of music.

The idea is that if two objects A and B are similar, then they can be
better compressed jointly than separately, so the difference in
compression length
D(A,B)=K(A)+K(B)-K(AB) is used as a dissimilarity measure.

I do not know of any other candidate (except for variants) that may
honestly be called a universal similarity.

I agree with you that the degree of similarity depends on the purpose.
This has been discussed at the Kolmogorov Complexity mailing list a few
years ago.

http://mailman.ti-edu.ch/pipermail/kolmogorov/2004q1/000112.html

One can show that D is smaller than any other computable distance
measure satisfying Kraft's inequality, but it is not always the right
similarity relation, with "right" meaning that it clusters w.r.t. to the
desired property (e.g. minimizing erroneous classifications).

So using "only" D might not be sufficient to perform a desired
classification task. So although D is universal in the mathematical
sense, this does not imply that it is universally good for EVERY
clustering or classification task

On the other hand, the experimental success of the universal metric is
remarkable. In the light of the above considerations it is even more
astonishing that the information-theoretic dominant feature seems
often(?) to be the one which we are interested in. The above
consideration may also explain why D (or variants) sometimes fail. It
would be great if one could augment or adapt D to the classification
problem at hand in a theoretically elegant way to allow for grouping
w.r.t. the desired property.

Best,

Marcus
